findings.description: The EC2 user_data script contains a plaintext AWS access key ID and secret access key. Anyone with DescribeInstanceAttribute/console access to this instance can read these long-lived credentials, and they are also committed to source control.

No metadata_options block is defined, so the instance uses the default IMDS configuration which allows IMDSv1 (unauthenticated token-less requests). Combined with the public-facing web server, an SSRF vulnerability in the application could be leveraged to steal instance credentials.

The encrypted attribute is commented out, leaving the EBS volume unencrypted by default. Data at rest on this volume (attached to the web host) is not protected against unauthorized access to the underlying storage.
This snapshot is created from the unencrypted web_host_storage volume, so the resulting snapshot is also unencrypted, exposing data at rest and any copies/shares made from it.
The security group allows inbound TCP port 22 (SSH) from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing administrative access to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks against the instance.

The security group's egress rule allows all protocols and ports to any destination (0.0.0.0/0), providing no restriction against data exfiltration or command-and-control traffic from a compromised instance.
The S3 bucket storing VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration (server_side_encryption_configuration), leaving log data unencrypted at rest by default.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block or bucket policy is defined for this bucket, so it relies entirely on default ACLs rather than an explicit guardrail preventing public exposure of flow log data.
